title: Create an empty calibration set instead of erroring
description:
closes #570

This PR adds a mock calibration split which returns the (outer) analysis set as the (inner) analysis set and an empty, i.e., 0-row calibration set. This is used when the calibration split isn't possible, e.g., if there is only one row in the analysis set.

Below is an example with the Chicago data. A `lookback = 0` means we only have one period in the analysis set and thus can't split further using the principles we settled on. This is the slightly less obvious case corresponding to "only one row available to split". 

``` r
library(rsample)
data(Chicago, package = "modeldata")

chicago_r_set <- sliding_period(
  Chicago,
  index = "date",
  period = "month",
  lookback = 0,
  assess_stop = 1,
  step = 2
)

chicago_r_split <- get_rsplit(chicago_r_set, 1)

i_split <- inner_split(chicago_r_split, .get_split_args(chicago_r_set))
#> Warning: Cannot create calibration split; creating an empty calibration set.

# empty calibration set
assessment(i_split)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 50
#> # ℹ 50 variables: ridership <dbl>, Austin <dbl>, Quincy_Wells <dbl>,
#> #   Belmont <dbl>, Archer_35th <dbl>, Oak_Park <dbl>, Western <dbl>,
```

title: New subclasses and `inner_split()` methods for validation sets
description:
This PR adds `inner_split()` methods for the `rset`s coming from `validation_set()`. Those `rsets` can result from the `group` and `time` variants of `initial_validation_split()`. 

To be able to tell where they are coming from, this PR also adds subclasses for the `group` and `time` variant to the output of `validation_set()`: the `rset` objects and the `rsplit` objects within those `rset`s.

I'm looking for a second opinion on the naming of the `rsplit` subclasses for the `time` variant. 

The interfaces and the original (and deprecated) approach via `validation_split()` put the `time` neither as a prefix nor a suffix but rather _inside_ the more general name: `initial_time_split()`, `initial_validation_time_split()`, `validation_time_split()`, and `val_time_split`.

I don't think we are going to touch the naming of the interfaces but we could touch the naming convention for the `rsplit` class. I've broken with that particular pattern of placing `time` and instead aligned with the pattern for `group`, i.e., used it as a prefix. Could be good, could be bad, could actually not matter much. 

The only place I think it'll matter is here and I'm happy to add a method for `val_time_split` to support the usage of the deprecated `validation_time_split()` if we think it's necessary. 
Edit: [this search](https://github.com/search?q=org%3Atidymodels%20val_time_split&type=code) suggests that we don't dispatch on that class elsewhere so it should only matter here.

title: Add `inner_split()` methods for bootstrap
description:
Unlike the `inner_split()` methods in #483, it's not straightforward what the splitting mechanism should be here.

Our main concern is data leakage:
The bootrap sample in `boot_split` or `group_boot_split` likely contains several replications of an observation. We don't want those to be split up into the inner analysis _and_ inner assessment set. Option 1 in the graph below is an example of that.

Options 2 and 3 in the graph try to avoid this by
- Option 2: do a grouped resampling with the row ID as the group (or for `group_boot_split`, the original group combined with the row id). This would mean that rows in the inner assessment set are potentially not unique, unlike the typical bootstrap OOB sample.
- Option3: sample with replacement from the pool of _unique_ rows in the (outer) analysis set. This prevents the two gripes we have with options 1 and 2. The inner analysis set is not sampled exactly from the same distribution as the outer analysis set but it can't be per definition? It is fairly close though?

Further thoughts:
With each bootrap sampling, we essentially put 1/3 into the assessment set. This could hurt us quickly, especially for small data. "Small data" is a problem for all other sampling procedures as well, but they usually have a dial to turn to affect that proportion. 
People could abandon fidelity to the bootstrap idea here by specifying a different sampling procedure for the inner split in `add_tailor()` when making their workflow.

Generally, this PR checks for empty dots via `rlang::check_dots_empty()` whenever they are documented as "not used".

For the `tidy()` methods, it was documented that the dots are not used. However, that was only true for some of the methods, see e.g., the tests for `tidy.vfold_cv()` which passed `unique_id` through the dots. Now all general methods (for `rsplit`, `rset`, `nested_cv`) have an explicit `unique_ind` arg and the dots have to be empty. The dots are generally documented via the rlang tag. Because that (also) states that the dots must be empty, the dots for a generic are documented with "Not currently used." only (since, for the generic, they do not need to be empty).

title: Validation split as a 3-way split
description:
This PR is the start of introduction functionality to work with a split into training/validation/testing as a 3-way split as opposed to two consecutive binary splits (testing vs not-testing and then not-testing into training and validation). Closes #369.

As an illustration of where this is going:
```
library(rsample)
data(ames, package = "modeldata")

# in this PR

# in the next PR
rset_for_tuning <- validation_set(first_split)

ames_val <- validation(first_split)
ames_test <- testing(first_split) 

# in the next PR
ames_analysis <- analysis(rset_for_tuning$splits[[1]])
ames_assesment <- assessment(rset_for_tuning$splits[[1]])
```

I'll comment on the code for specific things I'd like feedback on. 

In addition to that: Do we need methods for `obj_sum()` and `type_sum()` for `initial_validation_split` objects? I assume they are only needed for usage with pillar / within tibbles and we don't do that for initial splits?

Edit: Don't merge this yet, I'm collecting changes in this branch.

title: Add `validation_set()` for 3-way split approach
description:
This is part 2 of introducing a 3-way split approach to the validation split: This PR adds a function `validation_set()` to make an `rset` from the result of `initial_validation_split()` and `group_initial_validation_split()`.

The accessor methods are currently as follows, with `val_split` being the class of the split objects inside the `rset`:

 accessor / object           | `initial_validation_split` | `val_split`
---            | ---                        | ---        
`training()`   | training                   | training   
`validation()` | validation                 | validation 
`testing()`    | testing                    | error      
`analysis()`   | error                      | training   
`assessment()` | error                      | validation 

For other types of `rsplit` objects inside of an `rset`, `training()` and `testing()` will error (see #394). I've made them work here because the split object isn't actually resampled (all the sampling happens in `initial_validation_split()`) but I'd like a second opinion here! We can also make `training()` and `validation()` error on `val_split` objects.

Similarly, do we want accessor functions for the `rset` returned by `validation_set()`? For other resamples, these do not exist but for this case, it sorta feels like they should? Or more precisely: should it work because it's just one split in the set? This would also apply to the other sets with only one split: `validation_split`, `validation_time_split`, `group_validation_split`, and `apparent`. I can also open a separate issue on this if we want to ponder this further.

description:

``` r
library(rsample)
set.seed(11)

  group = 1:100,
  outcome = sample(c(rep(0, 89), rep(1, 11)))
)
observation_table <- tibble::tibble(
  group = sample(1:100, 1e5, replace = TRUE),
  observation = 1:1e5
)
sample_data <- dplyr::full_join(group_table, observation_table, by = "group")
group_mc_cv(sample_data, group, strata = outcome, pool = 0.1)
#> # Group Monte Carlo cross-validation (0.75/0.25) with 25 resamples using stratification 
#> # A tibble: 25 × 2
#>    splits                id        
#>    <list>                <chr>

#>  9 <split [74891/25109]> Resample09
#> 10 <split [74934/25066]> Resample10
#> # … with 15 more rows
group_validation_split(sample_data, group, strata = outcome, pool = 0.1)

group_initial_split(sample_data, group, strata = outcome, pool = 0.1)
#> <Training/Testing/Total>
#> <74869/25131/100000>
group_bootstraps(sample_data, group, strata = outcome, pool = 0.1)
```

title: Randomize strata
description:
This is a follow-up to #360 . I realized that the function was deterministic for any strata with only one group, and that it would always "short change" the last strata in the vector by giving it fewer folds as options (if `length(unique(strata)) %% v != 0`). Both of these strike me as small, but non-ideal bugs in the function; this PR changes the function so that the order of strata themselves are randomized, which I believe fixes both behaviors.

Sorry to pitch a breaking change right after we merged the first version of the feature -- I had this as a shower thought this morning and realized it wouldn't be that hard to change.

I made this reprex and I don't know that it's actually helpful at all, but here's proof that this stratified sampling works:

``` r
library(rsample)
set.seed(11)

group_table <- tibble::tibble(
  group = 1:100,

)

  observation = 1:1e5
)
sample_data <- dplyr::full_join(group_table, observation_table, by = "group")

strata_rate <- purrr::map(
  1:100,

    rs4 <- group_vfold_cv(sample_data, group, v = 5, strata = outcome)
    purrr::map_dbl(
      rs4$splits,
      function(x) {
        dat <- as.data.frame(x)$outcome
        mean(dat == "1")
      }
    )
  }
) |> unlist()

base_rate <- purrr::map(
  1:100,
  \(x) {
```

title: Add a first draft of stratification with groups
description:
Hi all!

Following some conversation in #317 I figured I'd post a first draft of what stratification with grouping might look like. This first draft _only_ handles `group_vfold_cv()` when `balance = "groups"`.

This version requires `strata` to be constant across all groups. If users have a non-constant variable they want to use for stratification, I think it makes sense to force them to create the strata (as I do in the example), because any automated binning implement will probably be non-optimal.

This implementation differs from `make_strata()` in that `strata` doesn't need to be quoted.

I'm not sure how you feel about putting the arguments after `...` -- because I only added `strata` and `pool`, and didn't include `breaks`, `nunique`, or `depth`, I didn't want to let people pass stratification arguments by position in case those other arguments get added later.

Addresses #317

title: Add `group_initial_split()` and `group_validation_split()`
description:
This PR adds `group_initial_split()` and `group_validation_split()`. These are documented as part of `initial_split()` and `validation_split()`, and don't have their own classes, in order to match the time-based methods. We might consider doing the same for `group_vfold_cv()` and `group_mc_cv()` (or, possibly changing these to use their own classes). 

It also fixes a bug where `group_mc_cv(..., times = 1)` would never produce an assessment set, because all data would be assigned to the same fold.

``` r
library(rsample)

set.seed(2)
dat1 <- data.frame(a = 1:20, b = letters[1:20], c = rep(1:4, 5))

group_initial_split(dat1, c) |> 
  testing()
#>     a b c
#> 1   1 a 1
#> 5   5 e 1
#> 9   9 i 1
#> 13 13 m 1
#> 17 17 q 1

group_initial_split(dat1, c) |> 
  testing()
#>     a b c
#> 2   2 b 2
#> 6   6 f 2
#> 10 10 j 2
#> 14 14 n 2
#> 18 18 r 2

group_validation_split(dat1, c)$splits[[1]] |> 
  assessment()
#>     a b c
#> 4   4 d 4
#> 8   8 h 4
#> 12 12 l 4
#> 16 16 p 4
#> 20 20 t 4

group_validation_split(dat1, c)$splits[[1]] |> 
  assessment()
#>     a b c
#> 3   3 c 3
#> 7   7 g 3
#> 11 11 k 3
#> 15 15 o 3
#> 19 19 s 3
```

title: Add `group_mc_cv()`
description:
This PR addresses #207 by adding a new function, `group_mc_cv()`, which can be used to create grouped Monte Carlo cross-validation resamples. Note that the user-facing function doesn't have a `balance` argument, because it doesn't make sense to balance anything other than the proportion of data assigned to the assessment fold.

This PR _also_ re-organizes code so that grouped functions now live in the same file as their ungrouped variants. I _believe_ we were agreed that would make the most sense going forward, but happy to undo if not.

``` r
library(rsample)
data(ames, package = "modeldata")
set.seed(123)
group_mc_cv(ames, group = Neighborhood, times = 5)
#> # Grouped Monte Carlo cross-validation (0.75/0.25) with 5 resamples  
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   splits             id       
#>   <list>             <chr>    
#> 1 <split [2182/748]> Resample1
#> 2 <split [2196/734]> Resample2
#> 3 <split [1980/950]> Resample3
#> 4 <split [2056/874]> Resample4
#> 5 <split [2178/752]> Resample5
```

title: Add new balance implementation
description:
This PR starts to replace what we removed in #310 (which undid #300), adding in a more flexible interface for balancing groups.

These new methods are both stochastic but have a similar interface to what was removed (`balance = "groups"` or `balance = "observations"`)

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(rsample)
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))

data(ames, package = "modeldata")
set.seed(123)

# Standard usage
group_vfold_cv(ames, Neighborhood, 5)
#> # Group 5-fold cross-validation 
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   splits             id       
#>   <list>             <chr>    
#> 1 <split [2449/481]> Resample1
#> 2 <split [2642/288]> Resample2
#> 3 <split [2218/712]> Resample3
#> 4 <split [2367/563]> Resample4
#> 5 <split [2044/886]> Resample5

# Equivalent:
group_vfold_cv(ames, Neighborhood, 5, balance = "groups")
#> # Group 5-fold cross-validation 
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   splits              id       
#>   <list>              <chr>    
#> 1 <split [2361/569]>  Resample1
#> 2 <split [2549/381]>  Resample2
#> 3 <split [2456/474]>  Resample3
#> 4 <split [2549/381]>  Resample4
#> 5 <split [1805/1125]> Resample5

# Alternative balancing:
group_vfold_cv(ames, Neighborhood, 5, balance = "observations")
#> # Group 5-fold cross-validation 
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   splits             id       
#>   <list>             <chr>    
#> 1 <split [2350/580]> Resample1
#> 2 <split [2350/580]> Resample2
#> 3 <split [2357/573]> Resample3
#> 4 <split [2347/583]> Resample4
#> 5 <split [2316/614]> Resample5

# Prove that balancing observations, balances observations
# 
# Get the standard deviation of nrow(analysis) for both methods:
analysis_sd <- function(v, balance) {
  group_vfold_cv(
    ames, 
    Neighborhood, 
    v, 
    balance
  )$splits |> 
    purrr::map_dbl(~ nrow(analysis(.x))) |> 
    sd()
}

out <- tidyr::crossing(
  idx = seq_len(100),
  v = c(2, 5, 10, 15),
  balance = c("groups", "observations")
)

out |> 
  mutate(sd = purrr::pmap_dbl(
    list(v, balance),
    analysis_sd
  )) |> 
  ggplot(aes(sd, fill = balance)) + 
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, color = "black", size = 0.3) + 
  facet_wrap(~ v) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(title = "sd() of nrow(analysis) by balance method")
#> `stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value with `binwidth`.
```

title: Refactor group logic
description:
This PR is a first step towards addressing #207 , by starting to factor some of the grouping logic out of `group_vfold_cv` and into its own functions. The broad goal here is to support additional functions (particularly `initial_split` and `mc_cv`) by expanding the `switch` statement with additional `balance` arguments. 

This PR shouldn't add any new features or change any behavior, but just reorganizes the grouping internals so that future changes are less invasive. It doesn't need to get in pre-1.0.0, there's no rush here.

title: Support variables in args for `nested_cv()` call objects
description:
Closes #81 


I spent some time today working on this (very old) issue and I _think_ this is the best solution. In the example shared, the values such as `outer_cv <- 5` are not in the call but in the calling environment.

One thing that confuses me a bit is that the *default* for `eval_tidy()` is `rlang::caller_env()` but if I don't explicitly set it like I do here, we still can't find those values.

Anyway here is what we get now:

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(rsample)

run_experiment <- function(all_dataset) {
  outer_cv <- 5
  inner_cv <- 4
  sampling1 <- nested_cv(all_dataset,
                         outside = group_vfold_cv(v = outer_cv, group = "Rep"),
                         inside = group_vfold_cv(v = inner_cv, group = "Rep"))
  
  sampling2 <- nested_cv(all_dataset,
                         outside = group_vfold_cv(v = outer_cv, group = "Rep2"),
                         inside = group_vfold_cv(v = inner_cv, group = "Rep2"))
  
  list(sampling1, sampling2)
}

all_dataset <- matrix(nrow = 50, ncol = 5, 0) %>% as.data.frame()
all_dataset$Rep <- 1:5
all_dataset$Rep2 <- 5:1
run_experiment(tibble(all_dataset))
```

title: Add vctrs support
description:
Closes #116 

This PR adds vctrs support to rsample. It is broken into 3 sections:

- Base R methods that have been added for supporting dplyr

- vctrs methods

- dplyr specific methods

It also adds an enormous test suite to ensure that the expected dplyr/vctrs behavior is happening for _all_ rset subclasses.

---

Base:

- `[.rset` was rewritten from the ground up

- `names<-.rset` was added

- I also had to special case `nested_cv`, so `[.nested_cv` and `names<-.nested_cv` have also been added.

All of the above generally take the approach of dropping back to a bare tibble any time any of the rset specific columns are modified or dropped in any way.

---

For vctrs:

- It looks like a lot of methods, but really they all repeat themselves. We have to do it this way because there is no inheritance in vctrs `vec_ptype2()` and `vec_cast()`.

- `vec_restore()` methods were added. These are called right before exiting from `vec_slice()` or `vec_ptype()` (among other things). The general idea is to always "restore" to a bare tibble rather than trying to restore to the rset subclass. This simplifies things considerably, and is generally the right approach because:

   - When you row subset an rsample subclass, it no longer has the correct structure. i.e. if you slice the first 5 rows of a 10-fold cross-validation rset, it is no longer a valid rset. So it makes more sense to return a tibble.

   - It influences the common types that appear in `vec_ptype2()`.

      - The common type of, say, a `<bootstraps>` with another `<bootstraps>` falls back to a `<tbl_df>`

      - The common type of `<bootstraps>` with `<tbl_df>` also falls back to `<tbl_df>`

      This is correct behavior because it affects things like `vec_c(<bootstraps>, <bootstraps>)`. Like with row subsetting, you probably won't have a valid bootstrap data frame after this (you'll have too many rows, and who knows if those two bootstrap data frames were even compatible), so the right thing to do is to fall back to returning a tibble.

- `vec_ptype2()` methods were added, but they abort immediately. These aren't strictly required, but I wanted to ensure that they really are never called because this is sort of an experimental idea. They aren't required because by having `vec_restore()` restore to a bare tibble, `vec_ptype2()` will never get the chance to dispatch off of `<bootstraps>`, so it should never see these methods.

- `vec_cast()` methods were added.

   - The following error. They will never be called "automatically" (because of how `vec_restore()` works), and would only ever show up if a user explicitly called `vec_cast()` directly. This is unlikely, and casting to a rset-subclass is essentially undefined, which is why these error.

     ```
     vec_cast(<rset-subclass>, <rset-subclass>) 
     vec_cast(<tbl_df>, <rset-subclass>)
     vec_cast(<data.frame>, <rset-subclass>)
     ```

   - The following are allowed. In things like `vec_c(<bootstraps>, <tbl_df>)`, when `vec_ptype2()` returns a bare tibble as the common type the `vec_cast(to = <tbl_df>)` method is used to convert the rset subclass to a bare tibble.

     ```
     vec_cast(<rset-subclass>, <tbl_df>)
     vec_cast(<rset-subclass>, <data.frame>)
     ```

--- 

For dplyr:

- `dplyr_reconstruct.rset()` works exactly like `vec_restore()`. Rather than restoring to a rset subclass after an operation like a row slice, filter, or left-join, we instead restore to a bare tibble because it is highly unlikely that we still have a valid rset subclass.

- `dplyr_col_modify.rset()` calls the default col-modify method from dplyr, then checks if we modified any rset specific columns. If we did, then we have to fall back to a bare tibble because the user has likely altered the column in a way that makes it no longer a valid rset subclass. Otherwise, we keep the rset subclass.

- `dplyr_row_slice.rset()` is not required because the default behavior is fine. It calls `vec_slice()` and then hands off to `dplyr_reconstruct()`, which strips the rset subclass.

Implications of these methods are that most dplyr verbs will return a bare tibble when used with an rsample subclass, but there are a few key ones that can retain the rset subclass:

- `mutate()` when the columns modified don't touch rset specific columns (`splits`, `id`)

- `select()` when the user retains the rset specific columns

- `relocate()`

- `rename()` when the renamed column isn't an rset specific column. Additionally if a column that starts with `id` is renamed, then as long as it still starts with `id` and doesn't duplicate any other column, it is still a valid rset.

title: Add `pool` argument to vfold_cv stratified sampling
description:
If you attempt to sample from strata that don't have enough examples, `vfold_cv`  bails out with a 'too little data to stratify' message and falls back to unstratified sampling. Sometimes we might want to force it to continue anyway – an example is given in #110. I also use this function on some unbalanced strata and want to ensure that a minimum of one example from each is included, even at the cost of some representativeness.

This PR achieves that by passing the `pool` argument through from `vfold_cv` to `make_strata`. Then you can use `vfold_cv(...,  pool = 0)` to force stratificiation to occur. The default value of `pool` is 0.15 which matches the value in `make_strata`.

Closes #110

title: `sliding_*()` resamplers
description:
This PR adds three new resampling functions, based on {slider}.

- `sliding_window()` is the most like `rolling_origin()`. It looks back a set number of rows to construct the analysis set, and looks forward to construct the assessment set. It doesn't deal with any time index whatsoever.

- `sliding_index()` is like `sliding_window()`, but it uses an `index` column to construct the resampling indices. For example, if the current row was on `2020-01-01`, the user could set `lookback = 20` to construct an analysis set that looks backwards "20 days" rather than 20 rows. This is useful if the `index` is irregular (has gaps).

- `sliding_period()` is my personal favorite. It takes the `index` column and a `period`, such as `"month"` or `"year"` and first constructs groups based on that period. Then it constructs the resampling indices based on those groups. Essentially this lets you create monthly / yearly resampling slices. It is a much better solution to https://github.com/tidymodels/rsample/issues/42

They are all in `R/slide.R`, which I think github won't expand by default since it is a little too long.

These generally replace `rolling_origin()`, but I don't think we need any immediate plans to deprecate it.

Closes #56 through the `complete` argument

---

An example of `sliding_period()` 

``` r
library(rsample)
library(modeldata)
data("Chicago")

# Break the resamples up by month:
# - Here we'll use an expanding monthly window by setting `lookback = Inf`
# - Each assessment set will contain two months of data.
# - To ensure that we have enough data to fit our models, we'll `skip` the
#   first 4 expanding windows.
# - Finally, to thin out the results, we'll `step` forward by 2 months between
#   each resample.
sliding_period(
  Chicago,
  date,
  "month",
  lookback = Inf,
  assess_stop = 2,
  skip = 4,
  step = 2
)
#> # Sliding period resampling 
#> # A tibble: 91 x 2
#>    splits           id     
#>    <list>           <chr>  
#>  1 <split [130/61]> Slice01
#>  2 <split [191/61]> Slice02
#>  3 <split [252/61]> Slice03
#>  4 <split [313/62]> Slice04
#>  5 <split [375/59]> Slice05
#>  6 <split [434/61]> Slice06
#>  7 <split [495/61]> Slice07
#>  8 <split [556/61]> Slice08
#>  9 <split [617/61]> Slice09
#> 10 <split [678/62]> Slice10
#> # … with 81 more rows
```

title: [WIP] pass alpha as param to get_p0
description:
IN #177 , @juliasilge mentions the bug may be a result of not passing alpha to `get_p0`.

This PR attempts to fix that. Here is the same minimal working example form #177 

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(rsample)
library(broom)


d <- tibble(x = rnorm(25)) %>% 
  mutate(y = 2*x + 1,
         noise = rnorm(25),
         Y = y + noise)


fit_model<-function(splits, ...){
  lm(Y~x, data = analysis(splits)) %>% 
    tidy()
}

set.seed(0)
bt<-bootstraps(d, 2000, apparent = T) %>% 
  mutate(models = map(splits, fit_model)) 


int_bca(bt, models, .fn = fit_model, alpha = 0.5)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   term        .lower .estimate .upper .alpha .method
#>   <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1 (Intercept)  0.817     0.929   1.00    0.5 BCa    
#> 2 x            1.64      1.73    1.82    0.5 BCa

int_bca(bt, models, .fn = fit_model, alpha = 0.05)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   term        .lower .estimate .upper .alpha .method
#>   <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1 (Intercept)  0.612     0.929   1.15   0.05 BCa    
#> 2 x            1.45      1.73    2.00   0.05 BCa
```

title: Validate single numeric value for alpha argument
description:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(rsample)
library(broom)

lm_est <- function(split, ...) {
  lm(mpg ~ disp + hp, data = analysis(split)) %>%
    tidy()
}

set.seed(52156)

car_rs <-
  bootstraps(mtcars, 200, apparent = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(results = map(splits, lm_est))

int_pctl(car_rs, results, alpha = c(0.05, 0.2))
```

title: Fix issue of when to generate the complement set
description:
Closes #188 

This issue boils down to the following behavior, which has to hold true for algebraic purposes, but can sometimes bite you:

``` r
out_id <- integer()

# are all values NA?
all(is.na(out_id))
#> [1] TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2020-10-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9001)</sup>

We used a check like this to determine if we needed to generate the `complement()` set or not. We actually wanted the empty set to be a "valid" assessment set, so in this case ideally we wouldn't need to generate the complement, but the check was returning the wrong result due to this `all()` behavior above.

Since our "signal" for needing to generate the complement is really just a single `NA` value from using `rm_out()`, I've added a `is_missing_out_id()` that just checks if `$out_id` is identical to `NA`. I then replaced all calls to this `all(is.na())` behavior with `is_missing_out_id()`, which fixes the issue.

title: Clustering approach to spatial CV
description:
Addresses #183.

This PR implements what I believe is the simplest and most straightforward approach that folks use for spatial cross validation. This is what the [sperrorest](https://github.com/giscience-fsu/sperrorest) package implemented (now no longer being actively developed) and what the [mlr group calls "spatial CV"](https://github.com/mlr-org/mlr3spatiotempcv#resampling-methods). This uses k-means clustering on the spatial variables to identify "chunks"; you can read about this [in this paper](https://doi.org/10.1109/IGARSS.2012.6352393); it is [what is shown in the plot here as well](https://bookdown.org/robinlovelace/geocompr/spatial-cv.html#intro-cv).

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(rsample)
data("ames", package = "modeldata")

spatial_folds <- spatial_cv(ames, v = 5, repeats = 2, 
                            coords = c("Latitude", "Longitude"))


plot_splits <- function(split) {
  analysis(split) %>%
    mutate(analysis = "Analysis") %>%
    bind_rows(assessment(split) %>%
                mutate(analysis = "Assessment")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(Longitude, Latitude, color = analysis)) + 
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
    labs(color = NULL)
}

plot_splits(spatial_folds$splits[[1]])
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/VXThU9D.png)

``` r
plot_splits(spatial_folds$splits[[2]])
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/EHlZw6W.png)

``` r

```

![](https://i.imgur.com/2joAF27.png)

<sup>Created on 2020-09-21 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9001)</sup>

If we wanted to do more complex spatial resampling like blocking, I think that will need to go in a separate package because of dependency issues like sf. This PR will be fine to keep in rsample itself.
